passage: So, I'm Himani, and this is the story of the night I nearly wrecked our school fest. Mum, whose name is Pallavi, said no to the evening rehearsal because it ends after dark. I said she never trusts me, went to my room and slammed the door. It felt good for about a minute. Then I heard her in the kitchen, not eating. The next morning I said, "I really need this rehearsal, it's the only time the whole group can practise. And I get that it's the road that scares you, not me." She looked surprised. I offered to share my location, message her when I left, and travel home with two friends. She said yes for the first three days and that we'd talk again after. Honestly, that was fair. 🙂

qa.q: Why did Pallavi say no to the evening rehearsal?
qa.a: She said no because the rehearsal ends after dark.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when Himani slammed the door, and what changed by morning?
qa.a: Himani felt controlled and angry, but hearing Pallavi not eating in the kitchen made Himani see the fear behind the rule, so Himani came back to talk calmly.

qa.q: Which parts of Himani's morning conversation would you copy?
qa.a: Himani stated the need, named Pallavi's worry about the road, and offered conditions such as sharing a location and travelling home with friends.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Himani said it was the road that scares her?
qa.a: She probably felt surprised and relieved to be understood, because Himani was answering her fear and not only fighting the rule.

grounding: A teen feels controlled by a parent's restriction, argues, then states the need, acknowledges the parent's fear and proposes conditions.

passage: I'm Jagdish, and I share a room with my sister Afreen. On Saturday she told Ammi she was going to the library. I know she went to the lake with her friends, because I saw the photos on a friend's status. When Ammi phoned, Afreen made her friends go quiet and told me afterwards, "Don't say anything." It worked for three weeks. Then Ammi saw the same photos. At dinner she said very calmly, "I would rather you asked me." Afreen stared at her plate. I can't tell what she felt: sorry, angry, maybe both. Next day I heard her say, "Ammi, can I go to the lake on Saturday? Here's who is coming." Ammi did not say yes right away, but her voice was softer.

qa.q: Where did Afreen tell Ammi she was going?
qa.a: She told Ammi she was going to the library.

qa.q: What might Afreen have been feeling at dinner when Ammi said she would rather be asked?
qa.a: She may have felt guilty and defensive at once; Jagdish cannot be sure, but she stared at her plate and looked both sorry and angry.

qa.q: What could Afreen do to keep some freedom without lying?
qa.a: She can ask openly, say who is coming and where, and agree on check-ins so that Ammi has reasons to trust her.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the library story when she found the photos?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and worried that Afreen could not be honest, since trust had been shaken, which fits her calm, quiet way of speaking.

grounding: A teen lies about where she is to avoid conflict, trust suffers, and she begins to negotiate honestly.

passage:
Tuesday night.

Papa took my phone for the week because of my marks. I didn't argue. I said "fine", came to my room and I've been here since five. Mum called me for dinner twice. I said I wasn't hungry.

I don't want to talk, because if I start I'll say something awful, or cry, and what's the point anyway. But sitting in here isn't fixing anything either. Papa doesn't know that what got me was "you're wasting your talent". It made me feel tiny.

Maybe tomorrow I'll say just one sentence: "I felt small when you said that." Only one. I can do one.

- Naveen

qa.q: What did Papa take for the week?
qa.a: He took the phone for the week.

qa.q: Why does Naveen not want to talk to Papa yet?
qa.a: Naveen is afraid of saying something awful or crying, and feels talking may change nothing, though Naveen also knows that staying in the room fixes nothing.

qa.q: What small step is Naveen thinking of, and how could it help?
qa.a: Saying "I felt small when you said that" names the feeling in one sentence, so Papa can understand what hurt and help.

qa.q: How might Papa see Naveen's silence?
qa.a: He may take it as anger or not caring, without knowing that "you're wasting your talent" made Naveen feel tiny.

grounding: A teen stops sharing with a parent and stays in the room, then considers naming the feeling in a sentence.

passage: I'm Samir. Kunal used to grumble that his father made him be home by nine, even when everyone else's curfews were later. Last night we were at my cousin's wedding and it ran late. Kunal's phone lit up. "Dad is outside," he said. "He has been sitting in the car for two hours because I said I might be late." He wasn't grumbling. He said, "I used to hate that rule. I think it was just him worrying." I can't know what he felt, but he was quiet all the way to the gate, and he thanked his father twice before he even got in the car.

qa.q: How long had Kunal's father been sitting in the car?
qa.a: He had been sitting in the car for two hours.

qa.q: What did Kunal seem to realise about his father's rule?
qa.a: He seemed to realise that the rule came from worry and care, not from wanting to control him.

qa.q: How could Kunal tell his father what he has understood?
qa.a: He could thank him plainly and, when the time is right, ask to talk about the hour as he grows older. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kunal's father see the nine o'clock rule?
qa.a: He probably made it out of worry, and waiting in the car for two hours suggests it was about care for Kunal.

grounding: An observer sees a teen realise that a parent's limit was care.

passage:
Monday. Gurleen opened Nilesh's profile before breakfast, again on the bus and again before bed. Every photo looked like proof that he was kind, funny and perfect. She imagined what he would say if she sat next to him at lunch.

Wednesday. She finally told her friend. "He hasn't replied to your story once," the friend said gently. "And he laughed when that boy dropped his tray." Gurleen said that meant nothing, but the tray part stuck.

Friday. At the canteen she really watched Nilesh. He talked over a girl, checked his phone while someone answered him, and forgot the name of the boy who had sat beside him all term. Gurleen still liked his smile. But the perfect person in her head was starting to look like someone she had made up.

qa.q: When did Gurleen open Nilesh's profile on Monday?
qa.a: She opened it before breakfast, again on the bus and again before bed.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say the tray part meant nothing, though it stuck with her?
qa.a: She wanted to keep her picture of him as perfect, but part of her had noticed something that did not fit.

qa.q: What small step could help Gurleen keep her feelings in proportion?
qa.a: She could keep noticing how he actually treats people, talk with friends she trusts, and spend less time on his profile.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's friend have felt about telling her?
qa.a: The friend was probably nervous but caring, and said it gently to help without hurting Gurleen.

grounding: A teen idealises her crush and checks his profile constantly, then a friend's comments and his real behaviour bring a reality check.

passage: After tuition, Gargi gave the boy from the front bench a folded note behind the cycle stand. He read it, said kindly but plainly that he did not feel the same way, and went home. Gargi's face burned all the way down the lane. That night she could not finish her roti and told her mother she had a headache. The next day she skipped tuition and hid in the storeroom of her aunt's shop. Her friend Neelam found her there among the rice sacks and sat down next to her without speaking for a while. Then Neelam said, "It hurts and it's embarrassing, but it isn't a verdict on you." Gargi cried into her sleeve. Over the next weeks the lane began to look like just a lane again.

qa.q: Where did Neelam find Gargi?
qa.a: Neelam found Gargi in the storeroom of Gargi's aunt's shop, among the rice sacks.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as she walked down the lane?
qa.a: She felt shattered and embarrassed; her face burned, she could not finish her roti and she hid the next day.

qa.q: How could Gargi's family and friends help over the next weeks?
qa.a: They could stay close, listen without teasing, keep her routine going and remind her that one no is not a judgement of her worth.

qa.q: Why might the boy have answered kindly but plainly?
qa.a: He probably did not want to mislead her or hurt her more, and being clear was a way of respecting her.

grounding: A teen is crushed and embarrassed after a no; time and a friend's support begin to heal, and rejection is not a verdict on worth.

passage:
Week one. Ramesh asked Jatin to send a photo whenever he was out, and said it was because Ramesh missed him. Jatin found it sweet.

Week three. Ramesh went cold when Jatin planned to watch a cricket match with his old friends. "If you loved me you would have stayed," he said. Jatin cancelled, and felt guilty for having wanted to go. He stopped answering his friends' calls.

Week five. Jatin's cousin asked why he had gone so quiet. Saying it aloud, Jatin heard how it sounded: photos on demand, apologies for seeing friends, guilt every time. Being missed was not the same as being watched. He decided to tell his cousin the rest and to talk to the school counsellor about what to say to Ramesh.

qa.q: What did Ramesh say when Jatin planned to watch the cricket match?
qa.a: He said, "If you loved me you would have stayed."

qa.q: Why did Jatin cancel and feel guilty for having wanted to go?
qa.a: He was mixing up Ramesh's jealousy with love, so he blamed himself for wanting time with his friends.

qa.q: What warning signs does Jatin notice, and what could he do next?
qa.a: He notices photos on demand, guilt every time and pulling away from friends, and he can talk to his cousin and the counsellor and get back in touch with his friends.

qa.q: How might Jatin's cousin see the change in him?
qa.a: They saw that Jatin had gone so quiet and were worried, and asking gently gave Jatin a chance to say it aloud.

grounding: A teen mistakes jealousy and monitoring for love and learns to spot control, isolation and guilt-tripping.

passage: I'm in the robotics club with Asif and Karthik, and I couldn't help noticing how they are. Before hugging Asif at the door, Karthik asked, "Is this okay?" and Asif said yes. Last week Asif said he wanted to skip the movie to prepare for his chess camp selection. Karthik said, "Then let's do the movie after. Want me to quiz you on openings?" When Asif got selected for the camp, Karthik said, "I'll miss you, but go," and he sounded like he meant both halves. I don't know what goes on between them when nobody is there. But nobody looked pressured, and both of them said what they actually wanted, kindly.

qa.q: What did Karthik ask before hugging Asif?
qa.a: He asked, "Is this okay?"

qa.q: What does Karthik's reply about the chess camp suggest he wants for Asif?
qa.a: He seems to want Asif to grow: he says he will miss him but tells him to go, though the narrator cannot see his private feelings.

qa.q: What can other couples learn from the way they handle plans and disagreements?
qa.a: They ask first, listen, say what they truly want kindly, and give each other space for their own goals.

qa.q: How might Asif feel about being asked first?
qa.a: He probably feels safe and respected, because his answer really counts. 🙂

grounding: A partner shows care that includes consent, space, honesty and support for the other's goals.

passage: Ten minutes before the annual day dance, Aditi's phone buzzed. Someone had sent her a screenshot: Ishita, her best friend since class six, had told the class group who Aditi liked. Aditi's hands shook. She still had Ishita's old voice note, the one where she cried about her marks, and her thumb hovered over the share button. Then the teacher called the dancers to the wings. Aditi put the phone in her bag, walked out and danced badly. After the show she found Ishita behind the stage and said, "You told my secret. I was so angry I nearly did the same to you, and I didn't. I need time to decide if I can trust you." Ishita went pale and said sorry.

qa.q: What was Aditi's thumb hovering over?
qa.a: It was hovering over the share button of Ishita's old voice note.

qa.q: Why did Aditi want to share the voice note, and what made her change her mind?
qa.a: She wanted to hurt Ishita back for the betrayal, but being called to the wings gave her time to cool down and she chose to speak privately instead.

qa.q: What might Aditi do next about the friendship?
qa.a: She can take the time she asked for, watch whether Ishita's apology is followed by more care with what she shares, and then decide how much to trust.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when Aditi said she had nearly done the same?
qa.a: She was probably ashamed and afraid of losing her best friend, seeing how much her telling had hurt.

grounding: A teen feels betrayed and wants to expose her friend back, but cools down, confronts privately and weighs whether trust can be rebuilt.

passage:
Monday. Hansa found out that Arohi had told the class she cried before the debate. Hansa did not answer her messages.

Thursday. Arohi waited outside Hansa's classroom and said, "I was showing off and I hurt you. I'm sorry. I won't tell anyone what you tell me again." She did not ask Hansa to say it was fine. Hansa said she needed to think.

Next Tuesday. They sat on the library steps. Hansa said, "I forgive you. But I'm going to keep some things to myself for a while, and you have to be okay with that." Arohi nodded, her eyes wet. "That's fair." They shared one packet of chips, and Hansa told her only about the exam.

qa.q: Where did Hansa and Arohi sit when Hansa forgave her?
qa.a: They sat on the library steps.

qa.q: What did Hansa want when she said she would keep some things to herself?
qa.a: She wanted to forgive Arohi but still protect herself, sharing less until trust has been rebuilt.

qa.q: How can Arohi rebuild trust with Hansa?
qa.a: She can keep her promise, accept the limits without pressure, and show over time that Hansa's words are safe with her.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel about the condition Hansa set?
qa.a: Nodding with wet eyes suggests sadness and relief; she accepted it as fair.

grounding: A teen forgives after a sincere apology while adjusting how much she shares; forgiveness is not forgetting.
